content: The implementation of basic United Nations (UN) vehicle safety regulations in key Latin American countries by 2030 could prevent numerous injuries and save many lives. A report by Global NCAP and the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) estimates that up to 40,000 lives could be saved and 400,000 serious injuries prevented if these regulations are adopted. Vehicles that meet or exceed UN safety standards significantly reduce the likelihood of road traffic crashes and the severity of injuries when crashes occur. However, only 40 countries currently comply with all seven priority safety regulations, which include seat belts, seat belt anchorages, frontal and side impact protection, electronic stability control, pedestrian protection, and ISOFIX child restraint anchorage points. To improve vehicle safety, it is essential to establish and enforce regulations that address these standards. Child restraint regulations, such as ISOFIX systems, secure child seats directly to the vehicle frame, enhancing safety. Motorcycle safety can also be improved through anti-lock braking systems (ABS) and daytime running lights. ABS prevents wheel locking during hard braking, maintaining stability and control, while daytime running lights increase motorcycle visibility to other road users, reducing crashes related to poor visibility. Enforcing traffic laws is critical to reducing road traffic injuries and fatalities. Key behavioral risk factors include speeding, drink-driving, not wearing helmets or seat belts, and improper use of child restraints. While many countries have laws addressing these issues, enforcement is often inconsistent or inadequate due to limited resources, lack of political will, or corruption. Effective enforcement strategies, supported by public education and communication campaigns, can improve compliance and save lives. Emergency care is another vital component of road safety. Timely and effective trauma care can significantly reduce deaths and disabilities resulting from road traffic injuries. Lowand middle-income countries, where emergency care systems are often underdeveloped, experience much higher fatality rates from severe injuries compared to high-income countries. Developing integrated prehospital and facility-based emergency care systems, including universal access to emergency services, can save lives and reduce the socioeconomic burden of road traffic injuries. Improving road safety also requires a long-term vision and strategy, supported by data collection and analysis to identify high-risk areas and target interventions effectively. In summary, adopting and enforcing evidence-based vehicle safety standards, traffic laws, and emergency care systems, along with targeted interventions for vulnerable populations like children, can significantly reduce road traffic injuries and fatalities.
